title: Nicodemus, New Birth, and God's Love for the World
summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night, and Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or from above, of water and the Spirit. Jesus speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the bronze snake in the wilderness, and the chapter declares that God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son. In the Judean countryside John the Baptist tells his disciples that he is only the friend of the bridegroom: he must decrease while Jesus increases.
story:
Chapter 2 ended with many in Jerusalem believing because of Jesus' signs and with Jesus knowing what was in them, for he knew what was in a man. Chapter 3 opens with “a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus” (verse 1), the first example of what Jesus knows. Nicodemus is impressed by the signs, and his conversation shows that admiration is not yet life. The chapter moves from a private dialogue by night to a public declaration of God's love and judgment, and then back to John the Baptist, whose ministry overlaps with Jesus' for a time in the Judean countryside. It is the first of John's long conversations, and it states themes that will run through the whole Gospel: new birth by the Spirit, eternal life as a present possession, believing and refusing to believe, light and darkness, testimony, and the lifting up of the Son of Man.

The chapter also closes the Baptist's part in the story. Chapter 1 had him point to the Lamb of God; here he gives his last testimony, calling himself the friend of the bridegroom whose joy is complete when the bride goes to the groom. Nicodemus disappears without a stated response, but he will return in 7:50-52 to ask that Jesus be given a fair hearing and in 19:39 to help bury him with a lavish weight of spices, so that his slow movement out of the night becomes one of the Gospel's quiet threads. Chapter 4 will set beside this respected teacher of Israel, who comes at night and struggles to understand, an unnamed Samaritan woman who meets Jesus at noon and brings her town to him.
historical:
The scene takes place in Jerusalem around the first Passover of Jesus' public ministry (2:13, 2:23), which on the forty-six years of 2:20 falls about AD 27 or 28. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law of Moses and of the ancestral traditions that applied it to daily life. Josephus, the Jewish historian who wrote in Rome in the last decades of the first century, describes them as the most accurate interpreters of the law, believing both in God's providence and in human responsibility, in the survival of the soul, and in reward and punishment after death (Jewish War 2.162-163; Antiquities 18.12-15), and he says that in Herod's day they numbered more than six thousand (Antiquities 17.42). They believed in the resurrection and in angels (Acts 23:8), which makes Nicodemus's inability to grasp a birth from above all the more striking. Archōn tōn Ioudaiōn, ‘a ruler of the Jews’, most likely means that he sat on the Sanhedrin, the council of priests, elders, and scribes that governed Jewish affairs in Jerusalem under the Roman prefect; he appears among its members in 7:45-52.

Nicodemus (Nikodēmos) is a Greek name, and Greek names were common among Jews of the period. Later Jewish sources know a wealthy Jerusalem family in which the names Nicodemus and Gurion recur. The Babylonian Talmud tells of Nakdimon ben Gurion, one of the rich men of Jerusalem before its fall in AD 70 (b. Taanit 19b-20a, b. Gittin 56a), and Josephus names a Gorion son of Nicomedes as one of the envoys who negotiated with the Roman garrison in Jerusalem at the outbreak of the revolt in AD 66 (Jewish War 2.451). Richard Bauckham (Journal of Theological Studies 47, 1996) argued that John's Nicodemus belonged to this family. The link is plausible but cannot be proved, and a reader should hold it lightly.

The second half of the chapter moves to the Judean countryside, where Jesus' disciples baptize (verse 22; 4:2 adds that Jesus himself did not), and to Aenon near Salim, where John the Baptist is still at work. Eusebius's Onomasticon, a fourth-century gazetteer of biblical places, puts Aenon in the Jordan valley eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth Shean), and the sixth-century Madaba mosaic map follows him; others have looked for it in Samaria, east of Shechem, where a village named Salim and abundant springs exist. The aside that John had not yet been thrown into prison (verse 24) assumes that readers knew of his later arrest by Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. Josephus says Antipas imprisoned and executed John at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea because he feared John's influence over the crowds (Antiquities 18.116-119). The aside also explains how this early period of overlapping ministries fits with Mark's statement that Jesus began preaching in Galilee after John was arrested (Mark 1:14). Only John's Gospel preserves this period, in which the two movements baptized side by side and their followers compared notes.

The dispute over purification in verse 25 belongs to a world in which ritual washing was widespread. The stone jars at Cana held water for purification (2:6), the Pharisees washed hands and vessels (Mark 7:3-4), stepped immersion pools (miqvaot) have been excavated by the hundreds in Jerusalem and Judea, and the community of the Dead Sea Scrolls practiced repeated washings while insisting that water alone cannot cleanse a person who refuses God's statutes (1QS 3:4-9, 5:13-14). A question about whose washing truly cleansed, John's, Jesus', or the customary rites, was a natural one to raise.
cultural:
Nicodemus comes by night. He may have wished not to be seen, as 19:38-39 suggests of both him and Joseph of Arimathea, or he may simply have come at the hour when serious study was done; the Community Rule from Qumran requires members to spend a third of every night of the year reading the book, studying the law, and blessing God together (1QS 6:6-8). John, who uses darkness and light as symbols from his prologue onward (1:5), means the reader to notice that this man comes out of the dark toward the Light, and the chapter's first discourse ends on exactly that note (verses 19-21). He addresses Jesus as Rabbi, a title of respect for a teacher, and speaks for others with his ‘we know’. Jesus calls him “Israel’s teacher” (verse 10), with the article in Greek, the teacher of Israel, a recognized scholar and perhaps a well-known one.

The images Jesus uses were at home in the Scriptures Nicodemus taught. Ezekiel had promised that God would sprinkle clean water on his people, give them a new heart, and put his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:25-27), and the vision of the valley of dry bones follows, in which the breath (ruach) of God brings the dead to life (Ezekiel 37:9). The book of Jubilees, a retelling of Genesis and Exodus from the second century BC, has God promise to create a holy spirit in his people and cleanse them (Jubilees 1:23), and the Community Rule looks for a day when God will cleanse a person with a holy spirit and sprinkle on him a spirit of truth like waters of purification (1QS 4:20-21). In Hebrew ruach, and in Greek pneuma, the same word means wind, breath, and spirit, which gives Jesus' saying in verse 8 its double edge. Later rabbinic law said that a Gentile who becomes a Jew is like a newborn child, in the sense that old family ties no longer count legally (b. Yevamot 22a), though we cannot be sure the saying was current in Nicodemus's day. Birth imagery for a new relation to God was therefore not foreign to Jewish ears; what startled was Jesus' demand that Israel's own teacher needed it.

The bronze snake of Numbers 21:4-9 was well known. When venomous snakes struck the grumbling Israelites, God told Moses, “Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live” (Numbers 21:8). Jewish interpreters were careful to say that the metal object did not heal. The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book written in Greek probably in the first century BC, calls it a symbol of salvation and says those who turned to it were saved not by what they saw but by God, the Savior of all (16:6-7); the Mishnah asks whether a serpent could kill or give life, and answers that Israel was healed when they looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven (m. Rosh Hashanah 3:8). The object itself later became an idol, and Hezekiah destroyed it, calling it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4). To be ‘lifted up’ on a pole would also make a first-century reader think of crucifixion, the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels, carried out in public where everyone could see.

The Baptist's image in verse 29 draws on wedding custom. The bridegroom's close friend, called in later Hebrew the shoshbin, helped arrange and conduct the marriage; the Mishnah defines a man's ‘friend’, in a list of those disqualified from testifying for him, as his groomsman (m. Sanhedrin 3:5). His task was to bring bride and groom together and rejoice at the groom's voice, never to claim the bride himself. The prophets had pictured God as Israel's husband (Hosea 2:19, Isaiah 62:5), so the Baptist is saying that Jesus is the bridegroom of God's people and that he himself is only the friend who brought them together. Jesus had just provided the wine at a wedding in Cana (2:1-11), and the image lands on ground the reader has already walked.
literary:
The chapter has two panels, each with a dialogue followed by a discourse: Jesus and Nicodemus (verses 1 to 21) and John the Baptist and his disciples (verses 22 to 36). The panels mirror one another. Both speak of one who comes from above (verses 13 and 31), of testimony given and not received (verses 11 and 32), of the Son sent by the Father (verses 17 and 34), of eternal life for the one who believes (verses 15-16 and 36), and of judgment or wrath for the one who does not (verses 18 and 36). The word anōthen frames the whole: its riddling use in verse 3 (again, or from above) is resolved by its plain sense in verse 31 (from above).

The first dialogue follows the pattern of misunderstanding that John uses throughout his Gospel (2:20, 4:11, 6:52, 11:12): Jesus speaks on one level, the hearer answers on another, and the misunderstanding lets Jesus say more. Nicodemus asks three questions (verses 4 and 9), each built on the verb dunamai, ‘can’, while Jesus answers with three solemn sayings introduced by ‘Truly, truly’ (verses 3, 5, and 11). The pronouns shift in a way English hides: Nicodemus's ‘we know’ (verse 2) is answered by a plural ‘you must be born again’ (verse 7) and by Jesus' plural ‘we speak of what we know’ (verse 11), so that the conversation widens from one man to a group, and through them to every reader. Nicodemus's voice fades as the discourse grows, and he is not heard again in the chapter.

Ancient Greek manuscripts did not use quotation marks, and interpreters disagree on where Jesus' words end and the evangelist's reflection begins. Some interpreters close Jesus' words at verse 15, and the ESV and NIV note that option in the margin, while those versions and the BSB run the quotation to verse 21; red-letter editions differ accordingly, and the same question arises in the Baptist's speech at verse 30 or verse 36. The shift from the first person to the third, and the use of the past tense (‘men loved the darkness’, verse 19), have led many commentators to hear the evangelist's voice in verses 16 to 21 and 31 to 36; others hear Jesus throughout. Either way the words carry the Gospel's authority, and the Gospel itself says that its testimony and Jesus' blend (21:24). The chapter also uses the word dei, ‘must’, for divine necessity three times: you must be born again (verse 7), the Son of Man must be lifted up (verse 14), he must increase (verse 30). New birth, the cross, and the Baptist's glad eclipse all belong to one purpose.

outline.t: Heavenly things and the Son of Man lifted up
God's love for the world; light and darkness
John the Baptist: he must increase
The one from above and eternal life

doctrines.note: “No one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (verse 3). New birth is God's work by the Spirit, as sovereign and untraceable as the wind (verse 8), and it is required of the most religious man in the room. Christians differ on how baptism relates to this birth (see the hard questions), but agree that no one can produce it by effort, heritage, or standing.

“For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son” (verse 16). The love is shown in its manner, a giving that reaches to the cross of verse 14, and in its object, the world that did not know him (1:10). The same verb returns for the Father's love for the Son (verse 35) and, darkly, for people who loved the darkness (verse 19).

The Son of Man must be lifted up as the bronze snake was, so that everyone who believes may have eternal life (verses 14-15). Israel in the wilderness was dying under judgment for sin, and God provided the means of healing on a pole; Jesus applies that pattern to his own crucifixion. John does not spell out a theory of how the cross saves, but he ties life to the Son's death and to faith's look at him.

The verb believe occurs eight times in the chapter. To believe in the Son is to have eternal life now (verses 15, 16, 36); to refuse him is to remain under God's wrath. Believing is pictured as the Israelites' look at the bronze snake: a trusting look at what God has provided, and in verse 33 as setting one's seal to the truthfulness of God.

Judgment is not only a future verdict but a present one. “Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned” (verse 18), and the verdict is that people loved darkness rather than the Light (verse 19). The Son did not come to condemn (verse 17), but to refuse him is to stay under the condemnation that already stands (verse 36).

words.note: Anōthen, from above, again, from the beginning. It occurs 13 times in the New Testament, five of them in John (3:3, 3:7, 3:31, 19:11, 19:23). BDAG gives both a spatial sense, from above, and a temporal one, anew or again. Nicodemus hears ‘again’ (his reply uses deuteron, ‘a second time’), while every other use in John means ‘from above’ (authority given from above in 19:11, the seamless tunic woven from the top in 19:23). Most commentators think Jesus means at least ‘from above’, a birth whose source is God, which is also a second birth; many think John intends both senses. English Bibles divide between ‘born again’ (KJV, ESV, NIV, BSB) and ‘born from above’ (NRSV).

Gennaō, to beget or to give birth, and in the passive to be born. It occurs 97 times in the New Testament, 18 times in John, and eight times in verses 3 to 8 alone, more densely than anywhere else in the Bible; 1 John uses it ten times for being born of God (1 John 3:9, 5:1). The prologue had already said that those who receive Christ are born ‘not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God’ (1:13). The passive voice matters: a person does not bear himself, and the new birth, like the first, is something that happens to us.

Pneuma, spirit, wind, breath. It occurs about 379 times in the New Testament and 24 times in John, six of them in this chapter. Like the Hebrew ruach, it can mean moving air, the breath of life, the human spirit, or the Spirit of God, and verse 8 uses it in two senses at once: to pneuma, the wind, blows where it wills, and so it is with everyone born of the Spirit. Verse 34 adds that God gives the Spirit without measure, which prepares for Jesus' promise of the Spirit in chapters 7 and 14 to 16.

Hupsoō, to lift up, raise high, exalt. It occurs 20 times in the New Testament and five times in John, always of the Son of Man being lifted up (3:14 twice, 8:28, 12:32, 12:34). Elsewhere it usually means to exalt in honor (Luke 14:11, Philippians 2:9). John uses both senses together: 12:33 explains that the phrase showed the kind of death Jesus would die, and yet the cross is the Son's exaltation and glory. The Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where the servant will be lifted up and glorified, may stand behind John's usage.

Monogenēs, one and only, unique. It occurs nine times in the New Testament: of an only child in Luke (7:12, 8:42, 9:38), of Isaac in Hebrews 11:17 (Abraham's unique son, though not his only one), and of Christ in John 1:14, 1:18, 3:16, 3:18, and 1 John 4:9. BDAG treats it as describing the only one of its kind within a relationship. The older rendering ‘only begotten’ came through the Latin unigenitus; Dale Moody (Journal of Biblical Literature 72, 1953) argued that the word comes from monos and genos, ‘kind’, not from gennaō, ‘beget’, and most modern versions followed the RSV's ‘only Son’. Charles Lee Irons (in Retrieving Eternal Generation, 2017) has argued that in John the word still carries a sense of derivation from the Father, and D. A. Carson has since moved toward that view; and the church's confession of the Son's eternal generation does not rest on the etymology either way.

Kosmos, world. It occurs 186 times in the New Testament, 78 of them in John and 23 in 1 John, far more than in any other book. It can mean the created order (17:5, 17:24), but in John it usually means humanity, and often humanity organized in opposition to God: the world did not know him (1:10), and the world hates his disciples (15:18). That God so loved the world is astonishing because of the world's hostility, not because of its size. The word occurs five times in verses 16 to 19.

Houtōs, in this way, so, thus. It occurs in verses 8, 14, and 16. In verse 16, “God so loved the world” most naturally means that God loved the world in this way, by giving his Son, rather than simply that he loved it so much; Robert Gundry and Russell Howell (Novum Testamentum 41, 1999) argued that it points back to the lifting up of verse 14. The degree of the love is not denied, but the word directs attention to its shape: a Son given and lifted up.

Orgē, wrath, anger. It occurs 36 times in the New Testament, but only here in John's Gospel (verse 36), and six times in Revelation. In Paul and Revelation it names God's settled, just opposition to evil, not a burst of temper (Romans 1:18). The present tense menei, ‘remains’, says that God's wrath is not newly imposed on the one who refuses the Son but stays where it already rests; the Son came to lift it, not to bring it.

christ:
This chapter tells who Jesus is and why he came. He is the Son of Man who has come down from heaven (verse 13), the only one who can speak of heavenly things from what he has seen. Agur had asked, “Who has ascended to heaven and come down?” and what is his name and the name of his son (Proverbs 30:4), and Jewish traditions told of Enoch or Moses ascending to receive heavenly secrets. Jesus reverses the order: the Son of Man descended first, and his ascent will be by way of the cross. The title comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where “One like the Son of Man” receives from God an everlasting dominion; in John the one who will be exalted is the one who must first be lifted up on a pole.

The bronze snake gives the pattern. In Numbers the people were dying under judgment for their sin, God provided the means of healing, and it was set up where everyone could see it; whoever looked lived. Jesus applies that pattern to his crucifixion, and the Greek word for the pole in Numbers 21:8 in the Septuagint is sēmeion, ‘sign’, the word John uses for Jesus' miracles. The link is typological rather than predictive: Numbers does not foretell the Messiah, but Jesus himself reads it as a picture of what he must do, and the church from the Epistle of Barnabas (12:5-7) and Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 94) onward followed him. Verse 16 then names the source: the Father gave his one and only Son, which many interpreters since the fathers have heard against Abraham's offering of “your only son” in Genesis 22, though John does not quote it.

He is also the bridegroom whose voice makes the Baptist's joy complete (verse 29), the one to whom God gives the Spirit without measure (verse 34), echoing Isaiah's promise that the Spirit of the Lord would rest on the shoot of Jesse (Isaiah 11:2) and on the servant (Isaiah 42:1). The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands (verse 35), a phrase repeated at the Last Supper (13:3). He came not to condemn but to save (verse 17), yet he is the dividing line: whoever believes in him has eternal life, and whoever rejects him remains under God's wrath (verse 36). The chapter holds together the gentleness of the Son's mission and the seriousness of the choice it forces, and it locates both at the cross.
interpretation:
The chapter shaped the church's language of baptism from the second century. Justin Martyr, describing baptism in Rome around AD 155, cites the saying that unless you are born again you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (1 Apology 61), and Tertullian, around AD 200, argued from verse 5 that the Lord had tied faith to the necessity of baptism (On Baptism 13). John Chrysostom preached on the chapter in Antioch in a run of homilies (Homilies on John 24 to 31), and Augustine treated it in Tractates on John 11 to 14, reading water and Spirit sacramentally and finding in Nicodemus a picture of catechumens who believe in Jesus but have not yet been reborn. The Council of Trent (Session 7, 1547, canons on baptism, canon 2) condemned anyone who says that natural water is not necessary for baptism and so turns ‘born again of water and the Holy Spirit’ into a metaphor. Calvin's commentary on John (1553) read water and Spirit as one thing, the Spirit who cleanses as water does, and on verse 16 remarked that the universal whosoever both invites all without distinction and removes every excuse from unbelievers.

The new birth became the watchword of the evangelical revivals. John Wesley's sermon The New Birth (1760, Sermon 45 in the standard collection), preached on verse 7, set justification, what God does for us, beside the new birth, what God does in us, and George Stebbins and William T. Sleeper's gospel song Ye Must Be Born Again (1877) carried the phrase into American revival meetings. In 1976, when Charles Colson published his memoir Born Again and Jimmy Carter spoke of himself as a born-again Christian during his presidential campaign, the phrase entered American political vocabulary, and Newsweek called 1976 the year of the evangelical. From about 1980 Rollen Stewart held up signs reading ‘John 3:16’ at televised sporting events, making the reference one of the best known in the English-speaking world.

Modern scholarship has argued over the water. Rudolf Bultmann (1941) thought ‘water and’ was added by a later church editor to bring the Gospel into line with sacramental practice, though no manuscript lacks it. Raymond Brown (Anchor Bible, 1966) heard baptismal overtones intended by the evangelist; Linda Belleville (Trinity Journal, 1980) and D. A. Carson (Pillar New Testament Commentary, 1991) read water and Spirit together as the cleansing and renewing of Ezekiel 36; Ben Witherington (New Testament Studies 35, 1989) took water to refer to physical birth. Dale Moody's article of 1953 on monogenēs shaped the rendering ‘one and only Son’ in most modern versions. Richard Bauckham's work on the Gurion family (1996) placed Nicodemus among the Jerusalem elite.

In the lectionary, the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1 to 17 on the second Sunday in Lent in Year A (as an option) and on Trinity Sunday in Year B, and verses 14 to 21 on the fourth Sunday in Lent in Year B. In art, Michelangelo gave the hooded Nicodemus of his Florentine Pietà (worked on from about 1547 to 1553 and intended for his own tomb) his own features, an old man hoping to be born anew; and Henry Ossawa Tanner, the first African American painter to win international fame, painted Nicodemus Visiting Jesus (1899) on a rooftop by lamplight after a trip to Jerusalem, a work that won the Lippincott Prize and hangs in the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. The Gospel of Nicodemus, a fourth-century apocryphal account of Jesus' trial and descent to the dead, borrowed his name as its supposed author, a sign of how his hesitant faith caught the church's imagination.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from manuscripts. In verse 13, Codex Alexandrinus, most later Greek manuscripts, and many Latin and Syriac witnesses add ‘which is in heaven’ after ‘the Son of Man’, which the King James Version translates; P66, P75, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus lack it, and most modern editions omit it, though a minority of scholars defend it as the harder reading that later scribes dropped. In verse 15 the earliest manuscripts read ‘that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him’ (en autō), while later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life’, making the verse match verse 16; the shorter text is almost certainly original. In verse 25 most manuscripts have ‘a Jew’, but P66 and the first hand of Sinaiticus read ‘Jews’. In verse 31 the first hand of Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae lack the second ‘is above all’. In verse 34 the earliest manuscripts say only that ‘he gives the Spirit without measure’; later manuscripts add ‘God’ as subject, and the King James Version supplies ‘unto him’ in italics, making explicit one reading of an open sentence.

Other differences are matters of translation. Verse 3 reads ‘born again’ in the KJV, ESV, NIV, and BSB and ‘born from above’ in the NRSV, because anōthen can mean either. Verse 16 reads ‘only begotten Son’ in the KJV and NASB and ‘one and only’ or ‘only’ Son in most modern versions (see monogenēs above). In verse 36 the KJV's ‘he that believeth not the Son’ renders a word (apeithōn) that most modern versions translate ‘rejects’ or ‘does not obey’, since it describes refusal rather than mere absence of belief. Where the quotation marks close, at verse 15 or verse 21, and again at verse 30 or verse 36, is an editorial decision, not a matter of manuscripts.

teach.big: No one can enter God's kingdom by religious standing; the life of the age to come is a birth from above, given by the Spirit to those who look in faith to the Son whom God, out of love for a hostile world, gave up to be lifted on the cross.

outline.t: Admiration for Jesus is not the same as life from God: Jesus answers a sincere compliment by naming a need Nicodemus did not know he had.
New birth is God's work, not a human achievement: flesh gives birth to flesh, and the Spirit, like the wind, cannot be commanded or traced, only received and seen in its effects.
Knowing the Scriptures is not the same as knowing their meaning; only the one who came down from heaven can speak of heavenly things.
The way into life is a look of faith at what God has lifted up: the crucified Son is the remedy for the poison of sin, as the bronze snake was for Israel.
God's love is measured by what it gave: the Son came to save, and the verdict falls already, now, on believing or refusing to believe.
The deepest reason people avoid the Light is moral, not intellectual: we fear exposure, yet the one who comes to the Light finds that what he has done was God's work in him.
Ministry is joy in another's increase: the Baptist refuses rivalry and finds his fulfillment in being the friend who brings the bride to the groom.
The Son speaks the words of God with the Spirit without measure, and everything turns on whether we receive his testimony: life for the one who believes, wrath remaining on the one who refuses.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first turns ‘born again’ into a label for one kind of Christian or one kind of conversion experience. Jesus says every person needs the birth from above, including the most devout; the text does not prescribe a dateable crisis, and people whose faith grew slowly, like Nicodemus's own, are not second-class. The second tears verse 16 out of its setting. Its ‘so’ points back to the lifting up of verse 14, and its love is the love that gave a Son to die; preached without the cross it becomes a general assurance that God is fond of everyone, which is less than John says. The third uses verse 17 (‘not to condemn the world’) to deny that there is judgment at all, when verses 18 and 36 say plainly that the one who refuses the Son is already condemned and remains under wrath.

Teachers should also avoid settling the water in verse 5 as if the text were obvious. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and many Anglican readers see baptism here; Reformed and Baptist readers often see Ezekiel's cleansing, and some see physical birth; each reading has serious defenders, and the teacher should say so. Avoid making the wind of verse 8 a warrant for spontaneity against order or for the claim that the Spirit's work is always dramatic; the point is that it is God's and not ours. Avoid treating Nicodemus as a coward or a villain; John follows him out of the dark with evident sympathy. And avoid reading verse 30 (‘He must increase; I must decrease’) as a call to self-contempt. The Baptist is full of joy, not self-loathing; his decrease is the gladness of a friend at a wedding.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people who fear they have never been truly born again because they cannot name a day or feel what others describe. Teach that the evidence of the Spirit is like the wind's, seen in its effects over time (coming to the Light, believing the Son, doing the truth), not in the intensity of one moment, and that the chapter's call is to look to the lifted-up Son, not to examine one's own inner experience endlessly. The scrupulous need to hear that the one who comes to the Light is not rejected for what the Light exposes. It also presses on people wounded by revivalism that used ‘born again’ as a test or a weapon, and on those who grew up in church and wonder whether their faith is their own; Nicodemus, a lifelong believer in Israel's God who came to Jesus slowly and at night, is good company for them. Those grieving someone who died without clear faith will hear verses 18 and 36 with pain; do not pretend the verses say less than they do, but remember that the chapter shows Jesus' patience with a slow and uncertain man, and that judgment belongs to the Son who came to save.

hard.q: If God loved the world, how can he condemn those who do not believe, including those who never heard of Jesus?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. Verse 16 speaks of God's love for the world, yet verse 18 says that whoever does not believe is condemned already and verse 36 that the wrath of God remains on him. The philosopher and theologian John Hick (God and the Universe of Faiths, 1973) argued that a God of universal love could not have made salvation depend on believing in a particular historical person whom most people who ever lived could not have heard of, and he concluded that the world's great religions are different human responses to the one divine reality. Many skeptical readers put the same point more simply: a love that condemns those who never had a chance is not love.

Christian responses divide on a second-order question. Restrictivists or exclusivists, such as Ronald Nash (Is Jesus the Only Savior?, 1994), hold that salvation comes only through explicit faith in Christ, and read verses 18 and 36 as the reason for the church's urgency in mission; they add that John describes a verdict already standing on a humanity that loved the darkness (verse 19), so that the Son's coming brings rescue, not the first condemnation. Inclusivists, such as Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God's Mercy, 1992), hold that salvation is always through Christ alone but that some who never heard of him may be saved by Christ through a faith that responds to the light God gave them; the Second Vatican Council taught that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel but seek God with a sincere heart may attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16, 1964), and C. S. Lewis pictured such a case in The Last Battle (1956). Within the tradition there is also the older argument between Arminian readers, who take verse 16 to mean that God's saving intention in sending the Son extends to every person, and Reformed readers such as John Owen (The Death of Death in the Death of Christ, 1648), who hold that God's love for the world issues in a special saving purpose for the elect while the offer to all remains sincere; D. A. Carson (The Difficult Doctrine of the Love of God, 2000) argued that Scripture speaks of God's love in several distinct ways that must not be collapsed into one.

What the chapter itself says is narrower than any of these systems. It speaks to those who have heard: the light has come, and to refuse it is to remain in the dark. It does not address the destiny of those who never heard, and Christians who confess that there is no salvation apart from Christ have held a range of views on that question. It also insists that condemnation was not the purpose of the Son's coming (verse 17). Readers should know that on this matter faithful Christians disagree, and that the church's confession binds them to Christ as the only Savior, not to one account of how far his saving reach extends.

hard.q: Does ‘born of water and the Spirit’ mean that baptism is necessary for salvation?
hard.a:
The case that it does is old and strong. From the second century the church read verse 5 of baptism: Justin Martyr (1 Apology 61) cites the saying in his account of baptism, and Tertullian (On Baptism 13) argued from it that the Lord had bound faith to the necessity of baptism. The Council of Trent (1547) condemned anyone who turns the words into a metaphor, and Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and many Anglican Christians hold that baptism is the ordinary means by which God gives the new birth, while also teaching that God is not bound by the sacrament in extraordinary cases. They note that John has just described baptizing by John and by Jesus' disciples (1:26-33, 3:22-26), so a first reader would naturally hear water as baptismal, and that Titus 3:5 speaks of the washing of regeneration.

Others read the verse differently. John Calvin, in his commentary (1553), took water and Spirit as a single idea, the Spirit who cleanses as water does. Linda Belleville (1980) and D. A. Carson (1991) pointed to the Greek, where one preposition governs both nouns, and to Ezekiel 36:25-27, which Israel's teacher should have known (verse 10): water and Spirit together describe the cleansing and renewal God promised, before Christian baptism existed. Ben Witherington (1989) argued that water refers to physical birth, matching the contrast of flesh and Spirit in verse 6. Rudolf Bultmann (1941) thought ‘water and’ a later editorial addition, a view few now accept because every manuscript has the words. Readers in these traditions note that the rest of the conversation speaks only of the Spirit (verses 6 and 8) and ties life to believing (verses 15 to 18, 36).

This is a second-order question on which faithful churches differ, and the positions overlap more than their polemics suggest: all agree that the new birth is God's work by the Spirit and that no one can enter the kingdom by human effort, and most who stress baptism also stress faith. A teacher should present the readings fairly and let the text's own emphasis stand: without the Spirit's work, no one sees the kingdom.

observe: What does Nicodemus say he and others know about Jesus, and how does Jesus respond?
What comparison does Jesus draw with Moses and the snake in the wilderness, and what outcome does he name?
What reasons does John the Baptist give for not resenting that everyone is going to Jesus?
interpret: Why might Jesus tell a devout and learned teacher of Israel that he must be born from above? What does that say about religious standing?
What does the lifting up of the bronze snake teach about how God saves and what faith is?
How can the Son come not to condemn the world while the one who does not believe is condemned already?
apply: Where are you most tempted to rely on what you know or what you have done rather than on what God gives?
John 3:16 says God loved the world by giving. How does knowing the shape of that love change the way you love people who oppose you?
The Baptist found joy in decreasing. Where in your work, church, or family is the increase of someone else hardest for you to welcome?
